clinicalPearls: A congenital eye movement disorder marked by limited abduction, globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction
Caused by aberrant innervation in which the lateral rectus is supplied partly by a branch of the oculomotor nerve owing to absence or hypoplasia of the abducens nucleus and nerve
Co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti on adduction pulls the globe back into the orbit, narrowing the lid fissure, with widening on abduction
Traditionally classified into three types by the pattern of abduction and adduction limitation (Huber types)
More common in the left eye and in females, and usually unilateral
Many children maintain binocular vision by adopting a compensatory face turn; amblyopia is relatively uncommon
Surgery is reserved for a significant anomalous head posture, manifest deviation in primary position, or marked up- or down-shoots
reference.pathophysiology: Duane retraction syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder arising from maldevelopment of the abducens nucleus and nerve. In the absence of normal sixth nerve supply, the lateral rectus receives anomalous branches from the oculomotor nerve. On attempted adduction, both horizontal recti contract simultaneously, retracting the globe and narrowing the palpebral fissure, while abduction is deficient because the lateral rectus is not properly innervated for that action. The condition is usually sporadic, though familial cases and the associated gene CHN1 implicate disordered axon guidance during brainstem development, and it can occur within broader syndromes such as Wildervanck.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital or acquired sixth nerve palsy
Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles
Congenital third nerve palsy with aberrant regeneration
additionalInvestigations: Orthoptic assessment of ductions, palpebral fissure changes and head posture
Cover testing for deviation in primary position
Audiometry and systemic examination for associated anomalies (e.g. Wildervanck, Goldenhar)
Neuroimaging if the presentation is atypical or acquired features arise
Genetic evaluation in familial or syndromic cases
redFlags: Acquired abduction deficit that could represent a true sixth nerve palsy needing urgent workup
Associated hearing loss or vertebral anomalies suggesting a wider syndrome
Amblyopia developing in the affected eye
A large primary-position deviation or head posture affecting development
reference.prognosis: Generally a stable, non-progressive condition with good functional outcome; many patients retain binocular vision via head posture, and surgery can improve alignment and posture though it cannot restore normal abduction.
pitfalls: Confusing it with a sixth nerve palsy and pursuing unnecessary neurological investigation
Attempting to restore full abduction surgically, which is not achievable
Neglecting amblyopia screening in unilateral cases
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
